nodes.value: Hard real-time, independent periodic and/or sporadic tasks scheduled by preemptive EDF on a uniprocessor; relative deadlines may differ from periods.
nodes.notes: The one-processor setting is stated in the abstract and EDF discussion; the system model itself also describes EDF preemption.

nodes.value: Periodic arrivals with fixed period T_i; the first jobs of periodic tasks arrive simultaneously.
Sporadic arrivals separated by at least T_i.
Earlier exact EDF utilization condition for periodic tasks with D_i=T_i.
nodes.notes: Prior-work result, not a restriction on the paper's main EDF model.

nodes.value: Earlier upper-bound result restricted to D_i<=T_i for every task.
Randomly generated task sets used for experimental comparisons of QPA and deadline-enumeration tests.
nodes.notes: Experimental generation policies are not formal assumptions of the schedulability theorems.

nodes.value: The set {τ_1,τ_2,...,τ_n} of n independent real-time tasks.
A task τ_i, periodic or sporadic, comprising an infinite or finite stream of jobs.
A released request or job of a task that must complete by its deadline.
One processor serving jobs under EDF.
A schedule dispatching a pending job with the earliest absolute deadline.
Interval during which the processor is busy.
Number of tasks n.
Worst-case execution requirement C_i per job of task τ_i; C_i>0.
Relative deadline D_i shared by jobs of task τ_i; may be less than, equal to, or greater than T_i.
T_i is the exact periodic interarrival time or the sporadic minimum interarrival time.
nodes.notes: Same notation, different arrival guarantee for periodic and sporadic tasks.

nodes.value: A job released at t has absolute deadline t+D_i.
nodes.notes: The symbol d_i also represents enumerated deadlines kT_i+D_i later; those are presented as analysis candidates.

nodes.value: Time instant or interval length t as specified by the surrounding demand expression or algorithm.
nodes.notes: Not all occurrences of t have the same role; keep argument scopes distinct.

nodes.value: Index k used to enumerate candidate absolute deadlines.
nodes.notes: Whether ℕ includes zero is not made explicit in the evidence.

nodes.value: Utilization of task τ_i.
Sum of the task utilizations.
The real-time tasks are independent.
Every task job must complete execution before its deadline.
If a periodic job arrives at t, the next arrives exactly at t+T_i.
If a sporadic job arrives at t, the next arrives at or after t+T_i.
nodes.notes: The inequality is a direct symbolization of the prose, not a change to the sporadic model.

nodes.value: The first job of each periodic task arrives at the same time.
Every job of task τ_i requires no more than its task worst-case execution time C_i.
All jobs of the same task share the task relative deadline D_i.
Preemption is allowed at any time; an earlier-deadline job may preempt a later-deadline job.
An arrived, pending job with earliest absolute deadline is selected for execution.
The main analysis does not constrain D_i relative to T_i.
All jobs of all tasks are guaranteed to complete their executions before their deadlines.
Candidate analysis deadlines are of the form d_i=kT_i+D_i with k∈ℕ.
nodes.notes: This is the candidate deadline formula used by demand analysis; sporadic jobs need not actually release at every such point.

nodes.value: Prior result attributed to Dertouzos: if the task set cannot be scheduled by EDF on one processor, no scheduling algorithm can schedule it.
nodes.notes: Cited result [9], not a newly proved theorem in this paper.

nodes.value: Earlier exact fixed-priority analysis computes per-task worst-case response times to evaluate schedulability.
nodes.notes: Background prior literature [2], [13]; no formula for its test is given.

nodes.value: Each task has D_i=T_i for the older periodic EDF utilization test.
Test total utilization at most one in the implicit-deadline periodic setting.
Attributed to Liu and Layland: a periodic task set with D_i=T_i is schedulable if and only if U<=1.
nodes.notes: Prior work [15], not original contribution of this paper.

nodes.value: Sum of C_i divided by min{D_i,T_i}.
Density at most one gives a sufficient EDF schedulability condition, not a necessary one.
Attributed to Liu: Δ<=1 suffices for EDF schedulability of the general task system.
nodes.notes: Earlier published result [16]; does not assert that Δ<=1 is necessary.

nodes.value: s_i denotes the start time of τ_i with min{s_i}=0; H is the least common multiple of task periods.
Attributed to Leung and Merrill: a periodic task set is schedulable iff all absolute deadlines in [0,max{s_i}+2H] are met.
nodes.notes: Historical result [14], not a theorem proved by this paper.

nodes.value: Maximum execution-time requirement of jobs whose releases and deadlines both lie within one contiguous interval of length t.
nodes.label: Equation (1)

nodes.value: For every positive t, processor demand is no greater than interval length.
Attributed to Baruah et al.: for sporadic task systems schedulability is equivalent to h(t)<=t for all t>0.
nodes.notes: Prior result [3],[4]. The paper later uses this demand condition in its general EDF analysis.

nodes.value: Upper bound L_a given by Equation (2), with the maximum deadline and the maximum T_i-D_i term.
nodes.label: Equation (2)
nodes.notes: Division by 1-U is undefined at U=1; the equation has no separate U=1 branch.

nodes.value: Test U<=1 and demand h(t)<=t over t<L_a with L_a from (2).
nodes.notes: The inequality in the displayed theorem does not write an explicit t>0 restriction; surrounding processor-demand interpretation supplies positive intervals.

nodes.value: Theorem 1 [3],[4],[5] asserts that the general task set is schedulable iff its utilization is at most one and the bounded demand test with L_a (2) holds.
nodes.label: Theorem 1
nodes.notes: Cited prior result. U=1 is stated although the bound formula has a 1-U denominator.

nodes.value: For the historical Ripoll bound, D_i<=T_i for each task.
Historical alternative upper bound written in the evidence as L_a^2.
nodes.label: Equation (3)
nodes.notes: Preserves the source notation L_a^2, not interpreted here as the square of L_a. Undefined at U=1.

nodes.value: The bound expression of Equation (3) is no greater than max_i(T_i-D_i)U/(1-U), as displayed.
nodes.notes: Read only on denominator-defined inputs; not asserted for U=1.

nodes.value: Alternate bounded-demand horizon from Equation (4), accounting for maximum relative deadline and weighted period-deadline difference.
nodes.label: Equation (4)
nodes.notes: This redefines L_a compared with (2); context and equation label distinguish the two. Undefined at U=1.

nodes.value: Check U<=1 and h(t)<=t for every t<L_a, where L_a is Equation (4).
Theorem 2 [7],[11],[12] gives necessary-and-sufficient schedulability using U<=1 and the bounded demand condition with L_a of Equation (4).
nodes.label: Theorem 2
nodes.notes: Attributed to prior work; the displayed L_a expression is undefined at U=1.

nodes.value: Busy interval starting with all tasks released simultaneously and thereafter at maximum rate; ends at the first idle period, possibly having length zero.
nodes.label: Definition 1
nodes.notes: Source definition credited to [18],[19].

nodes.value: Length L_b of the first synchronous processor busy period.
Initialize busy-period iteration by summing all task costs.
nodes.label: Equation (5)

nodes.value: Busy-period recurrence using ceilings of the current iterate divided by each period.
nodes.label: Equation (6)

nodes.value: Stop when two consecutive iterates coincide and return that value as L_b.
Compute L_b by initializing w^0, iterating the ceiling recurrence, and stopping at its fixed point.
nodes.notes: The source specifies the fixed-point stopping condition but no separate handling of a nonconvergent sequence.

nodes.value: Length of the synchronous busy period is the maximum length of any possible processor busy period in any schedule.
nodes.label: Lemma 1
nodes.notes: Prior source attributed to [19].

nodes.value: With EDF on one processor there is no processor idle time prior to an overflow (deadline miss).
nodes.label: Lemma 2
nodes.notes: Prior source attributed to [15].

nodes.value: Check U<=1 and h(t)<=t for every t<=L_b.
nodes.notes: The theorem displays t<=L_b without stating positivity in that line.

nodes.value: Theorem 3 [19] asserts iff schedulability under U<=1 and demand no greater than t for all t<=L_b.
nodes.label: Theorem 3
nodes.notes: Prior result attributed to [19].

nodes.value: At the synchronous busy-period endpoint, demand h(L_b) does not exceed L_b.
nodes.label: Lemma 3

nodes.value: Under synchronous maximum-rate releases, processor is busy throughout [0,L_b).
Assume h(L_b)>L_b, implying continued processor busyness at and beyond L_b, contradicting Lemma 1; conclude h(L_b)<=L_b.
Deadline candidates d_k=kT_i+D_i strictly less than min(L_a,L_b), with k∈ℕ.
nodes.notes: Here L_a explicitly refers to Equation (4); the theorem checks deadlines, not every real-valued time instant.

nodes.value: Check U<=1 and h(t)<=t at every deadline candidate t in P.
Theorem 4 [5],[7],[11],[12],[19]: schedulability iff U<=1 and h(t)<=t for every absolute deadline in P.
nodes.label: Theorem 4
nodes.notes: Referenced prior exact test; truncation bound uses min(L_a,L_b), strictly. E045 states h(t) can change only at absolute deadlines.

nodes.value: Piecewise QPA upper horizon uses min(L_a,L_b) when U<1 and L_b when U=1.
nodes.label: Equation (7)
nodes.notes: L_a is not defined at U=1. This equation does not specify behavior for U>1 (which fails utilization check).

nodes.value: Smallest task relative deadline.
For an unschedulable system, the latest candidate deadline strictly within (0,L) at which h(d_i)>d_i.
nodes.notes: Definition presupposes an overflow deadline in the specified interval; the source connects this to exact schedulability.

nodes.value: Largest candidate absolute deadline strictly smaller than L.
Smallest absolute deadline larger than d^Δ in Lemma 4.
Processor demand h(t) is nondecreasing in its interval-length argument.
nodes.notes: Stated in the proof, not separately proved in the Evidence Layer.

nodes.value: For an unschedulable system with d_m=max{d_i|d_i<L} and h(d_m)<=d_m, d^Δ<h(d^Δ)<d′, where d′ is the next deadline after d^Δ.
nodes.label: Lemma 4

nodes.value: Since the final candidate deadline d_m is not overflowing, the largest overflowing deadline d^Δ is earlier than d_m, and d′<=d_m<L.
Assume h(d^Δ)>=d′. The proof invokes monotonicity and a strict demand increase at the next deadline to infer h(d′)>d′, contradicting maximality of d^Δ.
nodes.notes: The evidence claims a strict increase from monotonicity; strictness is not established by monotonicity alone in the quoted passage.

nodes.value: For an unschedulable system with h(d_m)<=d_m, all t∈[h(d^Δ),d_m) satisfy h(d^Δ)<=h(t)<=t.
nodes.label: Lemma 5

nodes.value: By Lemma 4, for t from h(d^Δ) through d′ (exclusive), the demand remains h(d^Δ), at most t.
For t in [d′,d_m), an overflow would correspond to a candidate deadline d_k>d^Δ with h(d_k)>d_k, contradicting maximality of d^Δ.
nodes.notes: The source proof writes t^Δ once in place of d^Δ; retained as an unresolved notation inconsistency elsewhere.

nodes.value: Descending iterative schedulability algorithm: initialize t at the largest deadline below L; while h(t)<=t and h(t)>d_min, replace t by h(t) if strictly smaller or by the preceding deadline if equal; decide by h(t)<=d_min.
nodes.notes: Algorithm of Theorem 5. This is mathematical pseudocode, not a verified implementation. Precheck U<=1 is in the theorem, outside the displayed pseudocode.

nodes.value: Initialize the descending search at the largest candidate deadline strictly below L.
Continue while processor demand does not exceed current t and remains above the minimum relative deadline.
If h(t)<t, update t to h(t).
Otherwise in the loop, when h(t)=t, update t to the greatest candidate deadline strictly below t.
The algorithm returns schedulable if h(t)<=d_min; otherwise not schedulable.
Theorem 5: a general task set is schedulable iff U<=1 and QPA finishes with h(t)<=d_min.
nodes.label: Theorem 5
nodes.notes: Original paper result; theorem correctness claimed by source, not machine-checked here.

nodes.value: If an unschedulable task set has h(d_m)>d_m, the algorithm immediately stops on the overflow condition.
When h(d_m)<=d_m, the proof uses d_m>d^Δ and divides the descent into three cases.
Case 1 (h(t)<t): using monotonicity and Lemma 5, the t←h(t) step keeps t at least h(d^Δ).
Case 2 (h(t)=t): the preceding deadline step stays at or above d^Δ; choosing d^Δ exposes an overflow, otherwise the process repeats.
Case 3 (t=h(d^Δ)): the next earlier deadline is d^Δ and the algorithm stops because h(d^Δ)>d^Δ.
For every unschedulable task set the iteration maintains h(t)>=h(d^Δ)>d^Δ>=d_min, so stopping with h(t)<=d_min implies schedulability.
nodes.notes: This is the stated direction of the source proof; the theorem asserts an iff result.

nodes.value: QPA descends toward latest overflow deadline d^Δ for unschedulable sets and toward zero for schedulable sets if the early stopping condition is relaxed.
nodes.notes: Qualitative algorithm behavior stated in the paper; not a complexity guarantee.

nodes.value: For τ_j with D_j<t, the source gives the release time of its last job with deadline no later than t.
For task τ_j with D_j<t, last absolute deadline at or before t is floor((t-D_j)/T_j)T_j+D_j.
nodes.label: Equation (8)

nodes.value: If latest per-task deadline equals t, subtract T_j to obtain a strictly earlier deadline.
d_max^t starts at zero and is updated to the largest eligible adjusted d_j in the per-task scan.
Scan j=1,...,n; if D_j<t compute candidate deadline (8), step backward by T_j when equal to t, and retain the largest adjusted d_j.
nodes.notes: Pseudocode implements a STRICT predecessor via d_j=t adjustment; E076/E079 call the result a non-strict maximum (<=t), which is inconsistent in boundary cases.

nodes.value: The preceding-deadline scan has O(n) computational complexity, comparable with one evaluation of h(t).
The prose says that after the scan d_max^t equals max{d_i|d_i<=t}.
nodes.notes: Conflicts with E078 which subtracts T_j when candidate equals t.

nodes.value: The scan steps back when a candidate equals t, so its returned candidate is strictly less than t (if a valid previous candidate exists).
nodes.notes: Behavior follows directly from pseudocode, but existence of a positive candidate is not guaranteed by the excerpt.

nodes.value: Eight-task set with task parameters exactly as tabulated in the paper.
The eight-task example has U approximately 0.803, at most one.
Example: L_a=18000 (1735 deadlines), L_b=16984 (1638 deadlines), L=16984, d_min=16, initial t=16974.

nodes.notes: A worked example trace rather than a theorem proof step; represented as proof_step because the schema has no example category.

nodes.value: Worked example is classified schedulable after seven demand evaluations because h(t)=2<=d_min=16, against 1638 checked deadlines in the old approach.
Proposed tighter upper bound L_a^* incorporates max(D_i-T_i) and weighted T_i-D_i term.
nodes.label: Equation (9)
nodes.notes: No deadline/period restriction; denominator undefined when U=1. Definition is source-stated, not simplified.

nodes.value: Set of candidate deadlines d_k=kT_i+D_i strictly below L_a^*.
Check U<=1 and h(t)<=t for all t in the improved deadline set P.
Theorem 6: general EDF task set schedulable iff U<=1 and h(t)<=t at every deadline strictly below the improved bound L_a^*.
nodes.label: Theorem 6
nodes.notes: Source proof includes division by 1-U; the U=1 branch of this theorem is not addressed in the bound definition.

nodes.value: When t>=max_i(D_i-T_i), each floor((t-D_i)/T_i) is at least -1, so the maximum in h(t) can be removed.
With the floor terms nonnegative, the proof upper bounds h(t) by t sum C_i/T_i plus sum (T_i-D_i)C_i/T_i.
From an overflow t<h(t), the upper estimate yields t(1-U)<sum_i(T_i-D_i)U_i and, for U<1, t<sum_i(T_i-D_i)U_i/(1-U).
nodes.notes: The paper says U<=1 at E099 but divides by 1-U in E100; dividing requires U<1. This caveat is not a replacement of the source theorem.

nodes.value: For U<1, substitute L=min(L_a^*,L_b) into the QPA horizon selection.
Randomly generated task sets retained only if schedulable.
Randomly generated task sets that are unschedulable; older method searches deadlines in increasing order.
Generate task utilizations with UUniFast, described as giving a uniform distribution over 0–1.
nodes.notes: Experimental sampling method attributed to Bini and Buttazzo [6], not a schedulability proof algorithm.

nodes.value: Distribute task periods across exponential-width intervals e^0 to e^1, e^1 to e^2, etc., then sample uniformly within each interval.
nodes.notes: Period-generation method attributed to Davis and Burns [17]; stratification and remainder allocation are given in source.

nodes.value: Range factor comparing maximum and minimum generated periods.
For n=14 and period range at most 100, fix T_14=100; place the other 13 periods across five exponent intervals, two per interval plus three extras.
nodes.notes: Source presents the exact allocation of τ_1,...,τ_13 among the five intervals in E107.

nodes.value: Randomly sample each D_i in [a,b], with a=C_i when C_i<10, 2C_i when 10<=C_i<100, 3C_i when 100<=C_i<1000, 4C_i when C_i>=1000; default b=1.2T_i.
nodes.notes: Some experiments modify lower and upper bounds; these sampling rules are not formal model constraints.

nodes.value: Compare algorithms by number of evaluations of the processor demand function h(t); for the old method count checked absolute deadlines.
nodes.notes: Source neglects sorting cost for old unschedulable forward-order search (E129).

nodes.value: For old exact EDF testing, check deadlines within a bounded interval, in ascending order until a miss is found or all have passed.
nodes.notes: Old exact deadline-enumeration approach compared experimentally against QPA.

nodes.value: Each graph data point averages 6000 schedulable randomly generated task sets.
Each graph data point averages 6000 unschedulable randomly generated task sets.
Nearly all generated schedulable task sets in these experiments have Δ>1, so the sufficient density test fails to certify them.
nodes.notes: Empirical observation on these generated task sets, not a population-wide theorem.

nodes.value: Vary number of tasks at U=0.9, with a source-described maximum period-range parameter of 1000; results shown in Fig. 2.
nodes.notes: E116 writes Tmax=Tmin where other experiment evidence uses Tmax/Tmin; source wording is ambiguous.

nodes.notes: E118 also prints Tmax=Tmin rather than a ratio.

nodes.value: Vary total utilization for n=30, T_max/T_min<=1000; results shown in Fig. 4.

nodes.notes: E123 uses incompatible notation for b: see conflict node.

nodes.value: In 80000 schedulable task sets with U=0.9, n=30, most complete QPA in fewer than 30 evaluations, all fewer than 60, as described for Fig. 6.
nodes.notes: The period-range description E126 uses ambiguous Tmax=Tmin notation.

nodes.value: At U=0.9 and n=30, vary period-range parameter; comparison in Fig. 7; authors report larger advantages for ranges above 1000.

For n=30 and period-range setting 1000, vary utilization; results shown in Fig. 9.
Frequency experiment with 60000 unschedulable task sets, U=0.9 and n=30, shown in Fig. 10.
Across 80000 schedulable and 60000 unschedulable sample task sets, more than 96% of QPA checks need fewer than 30 h(t) calculations; previous methods average 65000 checks.
nodes.notes: Aggregate empirical observation; exponential reduction phrasing elsewhere is experimental, not a derived asymptotic complexity bound.

nodes.value: Authors state one evaluation of h(t) has O(n) cost, like evaluating total utilization.
nodes.notes: Per-evaluation complexity, not an O(n) worst-case bound for the whole QPA algorithm.

nodes.value: Paper reports exponentially lower calculation effort for QPA in almost all tested situations, with stronger comparative behavior across varied task sets.
nodes.notes: A source empirical performance claim; no worst-case exponential speed-up theorem established by this evidence.

nodes.value: Authors observed L_a^* dominating L_b when each D_i<=2T_i; suggest using only L_a^* if D_i is not significantly larger than 2T_i to avoid the busy-period iteration.
nodes.notes: Explicitly an experimental observation and practical suggestion, not a formal replacement for theorems or a proof of universal dominance.

nodes.value: For some unschedulable task sets the old ascending-deadline search can find a first miss sooner than QPA, but sorting costs additional work.
nodes.notes: E129 states a constructible example with 30 or more QPA iterations despite failure at first deadline; experimental comparisons ignore old-method sorting cost.

nodes.value: Several upper-bound expressions divide by 1-U, while their surrounding iff statements include U<=1; when U=1 those formulas do not evaluate.
nodes.notes: QPA Equation (7) gives an explicit U=1 fallback L=L_b; evidence does not provide a U=1 interpretation for Theorems 1, 2, or 6 as literally stated.

nodes.value: The predecessor pseudocode computes an earlier deadline than t when equal to t, but surrounding prose describes a maximum deadline at or before t.
nodes.notes: Do not silently change <= to < in source claims. The QPA algorithm needs the strict predecessor branch. At t equal to a deadline, the two operations differ.

nodes.value: Lemma 5 proof uses t^Δ in one inequality although the overflow threshold defined elsewhere is d^Δ.
nodes.notes: Likely a notation error, but source-faithful extraction cannot silently identify t^Δ with d^Δ.

nodes.value: Several experiment passages say Tmax=Tmin for a varied quantity, whereas neighboring definitions and experiments use T_max/T_min.
nodes.notes: The source does not consistently distinguish equality from a ratio; present experiment descriptions without asserting the equality as a meaningful constraint.

nodes.value: Default deadline-generation bound b=1.2×T_i differs in units/form from the later phrase b=max{D_i/T_i}=1.2.
nodes.notes: E122 expresses b as a multiple of T_i; E123 equates a time-valued b with a dimensionless ratio. Preserve original evidence.

nodes.value: QPA initializes t with max{d_i|d_i<L} and scans for a previous deadline, but the supplied evidence does not explicitly handle an empty candidate set.
nodes.notes: A domain/edge-case question, not a claim that the algorithm necessarily fails. Do not add an invented fallback.

nodes.value: Busy-period iteration gives a fixed-point stopping condition but no explicit behavior for an iteration that does not reach a finite fixed point.
nodes.notes: Do not infer from standard theory an unstated treatment of unbounded busy periods.
